papers.title_in_file: Quantum Hamiltonian Evolution for Coherent Quantum Learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:2609.03640v1, dated September 4, 2026 on the title page; a Supplemental Material appendix (pages 9 to 18) follows the Letter in the same text.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper with small simulations that proposes training a quantum model by evolving a register of discretized parameters under a loss-encoding Hamiltonian, with block-encoding constructions, a batched variant, and two simulated demonstrations (a classifier and a Mach-Zehnder phase estimate).

assertions.value: The authors introduce Coherent Quantum Learning (CQL), a training framework for quantum learning models in which the model parameters are quantum degrees of freedom evolved under a Hamiltonian that encodes the loss function.
quotes: We introduce Coherent Quantum Learning (CQL), a training framework for quantum learning models in which the model parameters are quantum degrees of freedom evolved under a Hamiltonian that encodes the loss function.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own framework in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the quantum case a parameter register initialized in superposition evolves unitarily, and probability amplitude concentrates near low-loss configurations through interference, without gradient computation or classical feedback.
quotes: a parameter register initialized in superposition evolves unitarily, and probability amplitude concentrates near low-loss configurations through interference, without gradient computation or classical feedback.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper's evidence for it is small numerical simulations.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no proof that the amplitude concentrates near low-loss configurations. The support is two simulated examples.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike general optimization frameworks, CQL is designed specifically for learning problems, where the objective function is generated by evaluating a parameterized quantum model on data.
quotes: Unlike general optimization frameworks, CQL is designed specifically for learning problems, where the objective function is generated by evaluating a parameterized quantum model on data.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own framework.

assertions.value: The authors discretize each trainable parameter with m bits, which gives a grid of two to the power m values in [0, 2π) (printed flat as 2m in the text layer), each represented by a computational basis state on m ancillary qubits.

of 2m possible values in [0, 2π), each represented by a
computational basis state |θ⟩ = |θ1θ2 . . . θm⟩ on m ancillary qubits.

assertions.value: The authors build on the time evolution of quantum Hamiltonian descent [28]: a Hamiltonian that is the sum of a kinetic term (a Laplacian in the parameter basis) weighted by one damping function of time and a diagonal loss Hamiltonian weighted by a second damping function of time.
quotes: We build upon the time evolution introduced in [28],

where eφ(t), eχ(t) are the damping parameters, Pˆθ2 is the Laplacian operator in the θ basis and HˆL(x, θˆ) is the diagonal Hamiltonian proportional to L(x, θ) that encodes the objective function to minimize.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the Hamiltonian it evolves under.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the exponent forms of the two damping factors flat; the value keeps to the words.

assertions.value: The authors remove the explicit time dependence of the Hamiltonian by the clock-dimension technique of Refs. [42, 43]: they enlarge the Hilbert space with a clock register, which turns the time dependence into a position operator, at the cost of a larger Hilbert space, and so obtain a time-independent Hamiltonian.
assertions.anchor: CQL protocol, Eq. (2), p.2; Supplement I, p.10
quotes: To address this issue, we employ the technique outlined in Refs. [42, 43], which involves enlarging the Hilbert space, introducing a “clock dimension” [44].
This expansion transforms the time dependence of a given Hamiltonian into a position operator Xˆt in an additional Hilbert space.
Consequently, albeit at the expense of enlarging the Hilbert space to Ht ⊗ Hθ, this approach enables us to work with a time-independent Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the method it adopts for the time dependence.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [41], that simulating time-dependent Hamiltonians is not a native operation in the circuit model and typically introduces considerable overhead.

assertions.value: The authors state that the complexity of training is transferred to the simulation of the dynamics generated by the time-independent Hamiltonian, and that throughout the Letter they assume access to a block encoding of the Hamiltonian and describe how to construct the novel components.

Throughout this Letter, we assume access to a block encoding of the Hamiltonian, and explicitly describe how to construct the novel components.

assertions.value: The authors propose to obtain the block encodings of the two damping factors by applying the Quantum Singular Value Transformation [49] to approximate them as polynomials, or by standard block-encoding techniques for diagonal operators, and to build the target Hamiltonian as a linear combination of the individual block encodings.
quotes: Next, one may apply the Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) [49] to realize a polynomial transformation to xˆt approximating the functions eφ(Xˆt), eχ(Xˆt)
the target Hamiltonian can be constructed as a linear combination of the individual block encodings.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction the paper outlines without a cost count.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using qubitization [34] to implement the time evolution of the initial state, they obtain a quantum state that encodes a probability distribution on the values of the parameter whose maximum corresponds to the optimal value for training the model.
quotes: we use qubitization [34] to implement the time evolution of the initial state.
we obtain a quantum state that encodes a probability distribution on the values of θ whose maximum corresponds to the optimal value for training our learning model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no proof or bound in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say how the optimal parameter is read out from the state or what the readout costs, and it gives no guarantee on the probability mass near the optimum.

assertions.value: The authors propose iterative batched training, analogous to mini-batch methods in classical machine learning, in which the dataset is partitioned into smaller subsets processed sequentially, and the parameter state evolved for one batch is the initial condition for the evolution under the Hamiltonian of the next batch.
quotes: We propose an iterative batched training strategy, analogous to mini-batch methods in classical machine learning, whereby the dataset is partitioned into smaller subsets that are processed sequentially.
The resulting parameter state is then used as the initial condition for a subsequent evolution under an updated Hamiltonian that encodes the next batch into the data registers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training scheme.

assertions.value: The authors state that a batch the size of the entire dataset (coherent global training) would require as many ancillas as data points, and that this is not a realistic scenario because it becomes impractical for large datasets.
quotes: this would require as many ancillas as data points. This is not a realistic scenario, as it becomes impractical for large datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit themselves.

assertions.value: The authors state that the choice of batch size introduces a fundamental trade-off between spatial resources (the qubit count) and temporal resources (the circuit depth).
quotes: Here, the choice of batch size introduces a fundamental trade-off between spatial resources, namely the qubit count, and temporal resources, namely the circuit depth.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no resource count is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the batched setting aggressive concentration of the state is undesirable, that the effective evolution time and the damping schedules play the role of a learning rate, and that the asymptotic divergence condition on the ratio of the two damping schedules, used in the global setting, is no longer appropriate and need not be imposed.
quotes: In the batched setting, however, such aggressive concentration is generally undesirable
In the present framework, the analogous control parameter is the effective evolution time under the CQL Hamiltonian, together with the associated damping schedules.
Consequently, in the batched regime, the asymptotic divergence condition on the ratio φ(t)/χ(t) is no longer appropriate and need not be imposed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A design rationale stated without analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the evolution time per batch is finite and the damping ratio does not collapse to zero within a single batch, the wavefunction keeps a non-zero kinetic dispersion, which introduces an implicit regularization analogous to a classical learning rate and avoids catastrophic forgetting across the training sequence.
quotes: This physical mechanism introduces an implicit regularization, analogous to a classical learning rate, preventing the state from freezing into a single batch’s local minimum, thereby avoiding catastrophic forgetting across the global training sequence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no experiment in the paper measures forgetting.
assertions.reader_inference: The numerical studies train on single-sample batches of one task and report loss curves; none tests retention of earlier batches against a baseline.

assertions.value: The authors give a batched CQL algorithm that, for each epoch and each batch, builds the batch loss Hamiltonian, evolves the state for a duration τ, and passes the resulting state directly to the next batch with no classical measurement between batches.
quotes: Evolve the quantum state continuously for duration τ
Note: The resulting state |Ψ⟩ is passed directly as the starting point for the next batch (No classical measurement intermediary!);
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full Hamiltonian needs block encodings of the clock momentum, the squared parameter momentum, the two diagonal damping functions and the loss Hamiltonian, assembled by tensor products, multiplication and linear-combination-of-unitaries techniques, at the price of an enlarged Hilbert space.
quotes: The price paid is the enlargement of the Hilbert space and the need to block-

the full Hamiltonian can be assembled using standard block-encoding arithmetic: tensor products for terms acting on different registers, multiplication for operator products, and linear-combination-of-unitaries techniques for the final sum.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction the paper outlines without a cost count.

assertions.value: The authors state that QSVT gives an asymptotically efficient block encoding of the damping functions when they are sufficiently regular, but that the cost can increase significantly for rapidly varying or nonsmooth coefficients, and that for a general function the Walsh expansion may contain many nonzero coefficients.
assertions.anchor: Supplement I A, p.10 and p.11
quotes: Thus, QSVT gives an asymptotically efficient block-encoding when the functions eφ(x) and eχ(x) are sufficiently regular, but the cost can increase significantly for rapidly varying or nonsmooth coefficients.
For a general function f (x), however, the Walsh expansion may contain many nonzero coefficients, potentially up to 2n, unless f has additional structure
assertions.certainty_reason: A cost statement given without a proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that in typical discretizations the norm of the discretized momentum operator scales linearly with the number of grid points, which is exponential in the number of qubits, and that this directly affects the cost of Hamiltonian simulation.
quotes: In typical discretizations, the norm of the discretized momentum operator scales linearly with the number of grid points, that is, as O(N ).
Since N = 2n for an n-qubit spatial register, this corresponds to an exponential scaling in the number of qubits.
This directly affects the cost of Hamiltonian simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement given without a proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that restricting the dynamics to a momentum subspace of bandwidth K replaces the worst-case norm bound, which is of order N, by an effective bound of order K, and that for sufficiently smooth or analytic solutions K can be much smaller than the number of grid points N.
quotes: restricting the dynamics to a subspace |p| ≤ K replaces the worst-case bound ∥P ∥ = O(N ) by an effective bound ∥P ∥eff = O(K).
For sufficiently smooth or analytic solutions, K can be much smaller than the total number of grid points N
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposed mitigation without a proof or a test in the paper.

time scaling like t ∼ ∆x (exponential with number of qubits).

quotes: The upper arm contains an unknown phase shift ϕ ∈ [−π, π), while the lower arm contains a controllable phase shift θ, which is dynamically updated by the CQL protocol.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the interferometric phase demonstration the probability amplitude of the parameter register is strongly localized around the optimal parameter value, corresponding to the unknown phase shift ϕ, by the end of the evolution, which they say shows phase estimation without repeated classical optimization steps.
